newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-QNI says 1st half profits to be down.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-QNI says 1st half profits to be down.

text.p: Nickel producer QNI Ltd said on Tuesday it expects to record considerably lower profits in the first half of the 1996/97 financial year due to lower metals prices and disruptions to ore supplies.

"The continued decline in the LME (London Metal Exchange) cash price for nickel to US$2.88 a pound at the end of December represented a decline of 17 percent since July 1996," QNI managing director Wyn Davies said in a statement.
Nickel has averaged only US$3.19 since July 1996, compared with US$3.83 a pound in the previous half year, Davies noted.
"The decline in the cobalt price has been more dramatic, with average prices in the first half being some 30 percent lower than the corresponding 1995/96 half year," Davies said.
QNI's financial year runs from July to June.
Continuing disruptions to ore supplies from mine sites at Gebe Island, Indonesia and New Caledonia have also weighed on production levels and costs, he said.

"Ore quality and supply for the first half of 1996/97 have been severely affected by continuing poor weather conditions at the Gebe mine site, which has impacted on supply schedules, ship loading, treatment costs and production levels at the Yabulu (Australia) refinery," Davies said.
QNI should produce just under 27,000 tonnes of nickel in 1995/96, which is in line with the previous year's output, QNI's chief financial officer, Christoher Foll, told Reuters.
"I would imagine that we'd be pretty close to last year," Foll said.
Weather and labour-related production problems that hurt production in the first quarter of the financial year flowed into the second quarter, Foll said.
First-quarter output was about 5,900 tonnes, he said.
"The second quarter was a bit better than the first, but it was still below average," he said.

Davies said that although its ore stockpiles had increased significantly by the end of December and nickel price had rallied in early 1997, these factors would only have a positive impact on the company's second half results.
"The nickel market is fundamentally sound," Foll said.
Some commodities analysts were forecasting average 1997 nickel prices approaching US$5.00 a pound. But Foll said he would be happy with a nickel price of around US$4.00 a pound this year.
